opus-5.5.text:
Thank you for having me. I think vision has played a really foundational role in the evolution of intelligence, and I like to start from biology. If you look back at the Cambrian explosion, around 500 million years ago, one widely discussed hypothesis is that the appearance of eyes was a major trigger. Once animals could see, the whole game changed. Predators could actively hunt, prey had to evolve ways to escape or hide, and suddenly there was enormous pressure to develop better bodies, better movement, and better brains to process all that visual information. So in a sense, vision and intelligence co-evolved, and vision was one of the strongest drivers.

What I find most important is that vision in nature was never just about "seeing" in a passive way. It was always tied to action. An animal sees something so that it can move toward it, grab it, avoid it, or eat it. Perception exists to serve behavior. That's why I think the loop of perceiving, deciding, and acting is really the core of intelligence, and vision is the richest input channel in that loop. It gives you geometry, physics, the material of objects, how things move, how they can be interacted with.

Now, if you compare that with the path AI has taken recently, it's interesting. Large language models have achieved remarkable things, but language is a very compressed, highly abstract product of human intelligence. It appeared very late in evolution. Before humans had language, there were hundreds of millions of years of animals that saw, moved, and manipulated the world. A lot of what we call common sense, like how a cup sits on a table, how a cloth deforms, how much force you need to open a door, is not really written down in text. It's grounded in visual and physical experience.

So from my perspective as someone working on embodied intelligence, vision is the bridge between the abstract world of language models and the physical world where robots have to operate. If we want machines to truly understand and act in the real world, they need to see in a way that is 3D, dynamic, and connected to their own actions, not just recognize labels in images. That's very much what we try to do in our research: make vision serve manipulation and movement, so that a robot doesn't just describe a scene, but knows how to do something in it.

I'd summarize it this way: language may be the crown of intelligence, but vision, together with the body, is its foundation. And I think the next big leap in AI will come from bringing that foundation back in.

r003.rationale: It says language appeared very late in evolution and describes animals seeing and moving for hundreds of millions of years before humans had language.

fable-5.1.text:
I think vision is probably the single most important trigger in the evolution of intelligence, and there's a very concrete piece of evidence for that: the Cambrian explosion. For about three billion years, life on Earth was mostly simple, slow-moving organisms. Then within a relatively short window, roughly 540 million years ago, almost all the major animal body plans appeared. One of the leading explanations is the "light switch" theory, that the emergence of eyes, of real image-forming vision, set it off.

Why would vision matter so much? Because once you can see, the world suddenly becomes much bigger. Before that, an organism basically only knows what it touches or what chemicals drift toward it. Its world is a few millimeters around its body. With vision, you perceive things that are far away, you perceive them before they reach you. That creates predators and prey in a real sense. You can hunt, and you have to escape. And that creates enormous evolutionary pressure, not just for better eyes, but for a brain that can do something with what the eyes see. You need to recognize things, estimate where they are, predict where they're going, and plan your own movement. So a large part of what we call intelligence, I think, grew out of the need to process visual information and turn it into action.

What I find striking is that the cost of vision is also very high. In humans, something like a third of the cortex is involved in visual processing in some way. The optic nerve carries far more data than any other sensory channel. Evolution doesn't pay that kind of bill without a very good return. The return is that vision is a general-purpose sensor. It gives you geometry, it gives you material, it gives you motion, it gives you other agents and their intentions. Almost everything you need to build a model of the world, you can get from light.

And that's why I think, when we talk about AI, the same logic applies. Language is very powerful, but language is a compression of experience that humans already had, and that experience was largely visual and physical. If we want machines that are not just reasoning over text but actually operating in the world, with robots and embodied agents, then vision, and more broadly spatial perception, is where that intelligence has to be grounded. In some sense, we're replaying the Cambrian story. Once machines can really see the three-dimensional world and act in it, I expect the diversity of what they can do to explode in a similar way.

r001.rationale: It says that before vision, organisms know what they touch or chemicals that drift toward them, describing perception without vision.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention sound or compare its place in the evolution of intelligence with vision.

r003.rationale: It describes language as a compression of experience humans already had, which it says was largely visual and physical, placing that experience before language.

astra-6.text:
I think vision has been one of the major drivers of intelligence because it allows an organism to anticipate what might happen before it makes physical contact with something. You can detect food, an obstacle, or a predator at a distance, and that creates an opportunity to choose what to do next.

But seeing isn’t simply recording an image. The organism has to work out which signals matter, how things are moving, and what actions are possible. So vision creates both an opportunity and a computational challenge. It rewards the ability to build a useful understanding of the environment.

What I find especially interesting is the connection between vision and action. You move, your view changes, and that change tells you something about the world. You reach for an object and discover whether your estimate of its position was right. That loop—perception, action, feedback—is a powerful foundation for learning.

I wouldn’t say vision is necessary for all intelligence. Other senses can support sophisticated behavior. But vision provides a particularly rich way to connect spatial understanding, prediction, and action, which makes it an important part of the story.

sol-6.1.text:
I think vision is one of the major forces that shaped the evolution of intelligence. Once an organism can see, it can detect opportunities and dangers at a distance. It no longer has to wait for something to touch it before responding. That creates a tremendous advantage, but it also creates a computational challenge: how do you turn incoming light into useful decisions?

To do that, you need to recognize patterns, estimate distance and motion, remember what you’ve seen, and predict what might happen next. And because the observer is moving too, vision has to work closely with action. You move your eyes or your body, the image changes, and you gradually learn which changes come from your own movement and which come from the world.

So I wouldn’t describe vision simply as a camera feeding information into an already intelligent brain. It helped create the pressures under which more sophisticated intelligence became useful. But it isn’t the only route. Other senses and forms of interaction also support intelligence. What makes vision especially powerful is the richness of the information it provides, and the way that information can guide action.
